analysis.body:
# Retail AI Adoption and Deployment

According to the Census Bureau, 15.5% of retail trade firms reported using AI in the latest survey period, up slightly from 15.2% in the prior period. This baseline measure, part of the Census BTOS series updated fortnightly, establishes that AI use in retail remains concentrated among a minority of businesses, though adoption is actively tracked and incrementally growing.

Retail AI spending is narrowing toward specific operational problems. IHL Group's 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands found that inventory data accuracy, not AI budget size, separates winners from laggards, suggesting retailers are shifting from experimental spending to targeted deployment. IHL also reports that most retail AI budgets fund the wrong layer first, with inventory distortion down to $1.7 trillion but empty shelves still costing $690.9 billion annually. This indicates vendors and money are concentrating on supply-chain visibility and inventory management rather than broader transformation. Aptos and Coresight Research report that 85% of retailers modernizing point-of-sale systems met or exceeded ROI expectations, with cloud-native tools lifting conversion and transaction values. A $1 billion retailer model projected $44 million in annual financial impact, demonstrating measurable returns in the subset of firms pursuing modernization.

Implementation examples show AI tools clustering around customer interaction and operational efficiency. Batteries Plus is deploying three AI tools across its 800-plus-location network: Savannah for franchise prospecting, Edison for bilingual customer call handling with SynthFlow AI, and Wattson for POS-connected product search, with full rollout expected by September 2026. This pattern reflects how mid-scale retailers are adopting point solutions rather than platform-wide transformation. JYSK is modernizing its SAP landscape on IBM Power Virtual Server toward S/4HANA to support expansion, AI, analytics and improved customer experiences across 3,600-plus stores, indicating that infrastructure investment precedes AI scaling.

Governance and compliance risks are emerging as adoption accelerates. IHL Group notes that "does it have AI?" does not predict pricing-platform quality among nine vendors tested, and retailers should instead test explainability on real items, control over automation by category and channel, and safeguards separating market-responsive from individualized pricing. This framing suggests that adoption without governance controls poses material risk, particularly where AI makes pricing or inventory decisions affecting consumers directly.

For retailers considering deployment, the evidence points toward caution about vendor claims and focus on measurable operational gaps. Coresight Research and the NRF both emphasize culture, influence and trust as prerequisites for moving AI initiatives beyond experimentation, implying that technical readiness alone does not ensure success. IHL's finding that inventory accuracy matters more than budget size suggests smaller retailers and specialists should start with data quality and specific pain points rather than expensive platforms, while larger firms modernizing infrastructure can expect meaningful financial returns if governance is designed in from the start.

https://ihlservices.com/.brief: IHL Group conducts research on retail technology spending and strategy. According to their 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, inventory data accuracy rather than AI budget size determines which specialty retailers succeed, and most retail AI budgets fund the wrong infrastructure layer first. The organisation also reports that inventory distortion has declined to $1.7 trillion, though empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion annually. IHL's analysis finds that the presence of AI does not predict pricing-platform quality among vendors, and retailers should instead evaluate explainability, automation controls, and governance safeguards.
